questions.sec: Renal failure flowchart & RPRF causes · p778
questions.q: Complete the classification flowchart of renal failure — 1) CKD  2) Non-CKD presenting over hours–days  3) Non-CKD presenting over days–weeks … A) Acute kidney injury (AKI)  B) Rapidly progressive renal failure (RPRF)  C) Chronic kidney disease
questions.exp: Flowchart: renal failure splits into CKD and non-CKD; non-CKD presenting over hours–days is AKI, and over days–weeks is rapidly progressive renal failure. (Book p778)

questions.sec: Renal failure flowchart & RPRF causes · p778
questions.q: Rapidly progressive renal failure (RPRF) is defined in the flowchart by a presentation over:
questions.exp: The flowchart timings: AKI = hours to days; RPRF = days to weeks. (Book p778)

questions.sec: Renal failure flowchart & RPRF causes · p778
questions.q: Match each cause with its place in the flowchart — 1) Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis  2) Hemolytic uremic syndrome  3) Severe acute interstitial nephritis  4) Atheroembolic renal disease … A) Causes of RPRF, some cases being atheroembolic
opts: All four are listed causes of RPRF
Only 1 and 2 are causes of RPRF
Only 3 is a cause of RPRF
All four are causes of AKI, not RPRF
questions.exp: Causes of RPRF listed under the flowchart: RPGN (due to glomerular pathology), hemolytic uremic syndrome, severe acute interstitial nephritis (AIN), and atheroembolic renal disease (some cases). (Book p778)

questions.sec: Renal failure flowchart & RPRF causes · p778
questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a cause of rapidly progressive renal failure?
questions.exp: ATN is the classic cause of AKI (hours–days), not of RPRF; RPRF causes listed are RPGN, HUS, severe AIN and atheroembolic renal disease. (Book p778)

questions.sec: Renal failure flowchart & RPRF causes · p778
questions.q: The flowchart attributes rapidly progressive renal failure chiefly to glomerular pathology.
opts: True — RPGN is listed first among RPRF causes and is due to glomerular pathology
False — RPRF is due to tubular pathology
True — it is due entirely to interstitial pathology
False — RPRF is defined by vascular pathology only
questions.exp: Under RPRF the first listed cause is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), annotated 'due to glomerular pathology'. (Book p778)

questions.sec: Renal failure flowchart & RPRF causes · p778
questions.q: RPGN is defined as RPRF plus:
opts: Diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with crescents on light microscopy
Diffuse mesangial IgA deposition with normal light microscopy
Acute tubular necrosis with muddy brown casts
questions.exp: RPGN = RPRF + diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis with crescents (an HPE/light-microscopy feature). (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: Match each urine feature of RPGN with its description — 1) Colour  2) Output  3) Urine analysis … A) Decreased output  B) Cola-coloured (RBC present)  C) Proteinuria +/– (trace to variable)
questions.exp: RPGN urine: cola-coloured with RBCs; decreased output; urine examination shows proteinuria +/–. (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: A 40-year-old man has a 3-week history of progressive puffiness around the eyes and legs, BP 160/100 mmHg, cola-coloured urine and reduced urine output. Which statement about these findings is correct?
opts: Periorbital puffiness with progressive oedema and a raised BP are listed features of RPGN
Periorbital puffiness with a normal BP is a feature unique to nephrotic syndrome
The progressive oedema of RPGN accumulates in the intravascular compartment
Cola-coloured urine with reduced output indicates isolated post-renal obstruction
questions.exp: RPGN features: periorbital puffiness, progressive oedema (extravascular compartment) and raised blood pressure, with cola-coloured urine and decreased output. (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: Fill up: In RPGN, progressive oedema accumulates in the ______ compartment.
questions.exp: Features of RPGN: progressive oedema (extravascular compartment), periorbital puffiness and raised blood pressure. (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: Raised blood pressure is a listed feature of RPGN along with periorbital puffiness.
opts: False — BP is normal in RPGN
True, but only in type III disease
False — BP falls as creatinine rises
questions.exp: RPGN features list ends with raised blood pressure. (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: A man with RPGN is examined. Chest auscultation is expected to reveal:
opts: A pleural rub with absent breath sounds
A pansystolic murmur at the apex
Bronchial breathing with a pleural rub
questions.exp: Auscultation in RPGN: scattered crepitations (from fluid overload/uraemic lung). (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: Which statement about blood investigations in RPGN is correct?
opts: CBC is normal, while serum creatinine and urea are raised
CBC shows marked leucocytosis, with normal creatinine
Serum creatinine is raised only if sepsis coexists
Serum urea is reduced with a raised creatinine
questions.exp: Blood investigations in RPGN: CBC normal; serum creatinine raised; serum urea raised; serum K⁺ normal or raised; ABG normal or metabolic acidosis. (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: Match each RPGN investigation with its expected result — 1) CBC  2) Serum creatinine  3) Serum K⁺  4) ABG … A) Normal/raised  B) Normal  C) Normal/metabolic acidosis  D) Raised
questions.exp: RPGN investigations: CBC normal; creatinine raised; serum K⁺ normal or raised; ABG normal or metabolic acidosis (serum urea also raised). (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN features & investigations · p778
questions.q: All but one of the following are typical laboratory findings in RPGN. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Normocytic anaemia with a low haemoglobin on the CBC
Raised serum creatinine together with a raised serum urea
Normal CBC with a raised serum creatinine and a raised urea
ABG showing normal pH or metabolic acidosis with normal or high K⁺
questions.exp: The CBC is normal in RPGN; creatinine and urea are raised, serum K⁺ is normal or raised and the ABG is normal or shows metabolic acidosis. (Book p778)

questions.sec: RPGN biopsy: light microscopy & IF patterns · p779
questions.q: The light-microscopy hallmark of crescentic glomerulonephritis described here is:
opts: Proliferation of parietal epithelial cells with fibrin, the number of crescents mattering
Segmental sclerosis with hyalinosis at the vascular pole
Basement membrane thinning with splitting of the lamina densa
questions.exp: LM shows crescentic GN due to proliferation of parietal epithelial cells with fibrin; the number of crescents is an important factor. (Book p779)

questions.sec: RPGN biopsy: light microscopy & IF patterns · p779
questions.q: Fill up: The crescents of crescentic glomerulonephritis are formed by proliferation of ______ epithelial cells with fibrin.
questions.exp: Crescents arise from proliferation of parietal epithelial cells together with fibrin; their number matters prognostically. (Book p779)

questions.sec: RPGN biopsy: light microscopy & IF patterns · p779
questions.q: Match each immunofluorescence pattern in the biopsy figure with its image label — 1) No deposits  2) Uniform bright linear staining along the capillary walls  3) Coarse granular staining of capillary loops and mesangium … A) Linear IF  B) Negative IF  C) Diffuse granular IF
questions.exp: The figure panels are labelled: A. negative IF; B. diffuse granular IF; C. linear IF (with D. granular IF) — the linear pattern being the one written in text for type I RPGN. (Book p779)

questions.sec: RPGN biopsy: light microscopy & IF patterns · p779
questions.q: Linear immunofluorescence in type I RPGN occurs because the antibodies are directed against a structural antigen of the glomerular basement membrane.
opts: True — linear IF is the imprint of anti-GBM antibody binding
False — linear IF is typical of immune-complex disease
False — linear IF in RPGN is due to cellular crescents alone
True, but linear IF is seen only in type III disease
questions.exp: Type I RPGN (Goodpasture syndrome) shows linear IgG ± C3 along the glomerular capillary wall, being anti-GBM antibody disease; the granular patterns of panels B/D arise from immune-complex deposition. (Book p779)

questions.sec: RPGN biopsy: light microscopy & IF patterns · p779
questions.q: Match each IF pattern with its listed important association — 1) Linear IF  2) Granular IF … A) Immune-complex deposition, e.g. diabetes mellitus and light chain disease  B) Goodpasture disease
questions.exp: Important IF associations: linear IF → Goodpasture disease; granular IF → diabetes mellitus and light chain disease. (Book p779)

questions.sec: RPGN biopsy: light microscopy & IF patterns · p779
questions.q: Which condition is NOT listed among the important associations of the immunofluorescence patterns?
opts: Goodpasture disease, associated with linear IF
Diabetes mellitus, associated with granular IF
Light chain disease, associated with granular IF
questions.exp: The associations printed are Goodpasture disease (linear), diabetes mellitus and light chain disease (granular); PSGN is not on that list. (Book p779)

questions.sec: RPGN biopsy: light microscopy & IF patterns · p779
questions.q: A diabetic patient with nephrotic-range proteinuria and renal failure has a renal biopsy showing coarse granular immunofluorescence; the listed important association is:
questions.exp: Granular IF is importantly associated with diabetes mellitus and light chain disease; Goodpasture disease goes with linear IF. (Book p779)

questions.sec: When to biopsy vs dialyse first · p779
questions.q: A patient with RPGN has a very high serum creatinine. The book advises against immediate renal biopsy because:
opts: It will not show crescents at this stage
The kidney is too small for a safe puncture
Immunofluorescence cannot be performed at high creatinine
questions.exp: Note: biopsy should not be done if serum creatinine is markedly increased, as it may cause uremic bleeding. (Book p779)

questions.sec: When to biopsy vs dialyse first · p779
questions.q: Arrange the correct sequence when the serum creatinine is very high — 1) First step  2) Then  3) If the value decreases … A) Recheck serum creatinine  B) Dialysis  C) Biopsy
questions.exp: When the creatinine is very high: first step dialysis → recheck serum creatinine → if the value decreases, proceed to biopsy. (Book p779)

questions.sec: When to biopsy vs dialyse first · p779
questions.q: In the high-creatinine RPGN algorithm, biopsy is performed:
opts: After dialysis, provided the rechecked serum creatinine decreases
Only when the creatinine exceeds 5.5 mg/dL
Simultaneously with the first dialysis session
questions.exp: Algorithm: dialysis → recheck creatinine → biopsy if the value decreases (avoiding uremic bleeding from an immediate biopsy). (Book p779)

questions.sec: When to biopsy vs dialyse first · p779
questions.q: According to the page, an immediately raised serum creatinine is an absolute contraindication to ever performing a renal biopsy.
opts: False — dialysis is done first and biopsy follows once the creatinine falls
True — biopsy is never repeated in such patients
True — biopsy then has to be replaced by CT imaging
False — biopsy is performed before dialysis instead
questions.exp: It is the immediate biopsy that is avoided (uremic bleeding risk); after dialysis, if the creatinine decreases, biopsy is performed. (Book p779)

questions.sec: RPGN treatment approach: check first · p780
questions.q: Match each first-line assessment in the RPGN treatment approach with what is sought — 1) ECG  2) ABG  3) Volume status … A) Metabolic acidosis  B) Signs of hyperkalemia  C) Inferior vena cava diameter on USG
questions.exp: Step 1 of the RPGN treatment approach: check ECG (signs of hyperkalaemia), ABG (metabolic acidosis) and volume status (IVC diameter on USG). (Book p780)

questions.sec: RPGN treatment approach: check first · p780
questions.q: In the RPGN treatment algorithm, the ECG shows signs of hyperkalemia. The recommended treatment is:
opts: Calcium gluconate IV 10 mL over 2–3 minutes
Insulin infusion with 50% dextrose over 2–3 hours
questions.exp: ECG signs of hyperkalaemia in RPGN are treated with calcium gluconate IV 10 mL over 2–3 minutes. (Book p780)

questions.sec: RPGN treatment approach: check first · p780
questions.q: Calcium gluconate in hyperkalaemic RPGN is given as 10 mL IV over:
questions.exp: Calcium gluconate 10 mL IV given over 2–3 minutes for ECG signs of hyperkalaemia. (Book p780)

questions.sec: RPGN treatment approach: check first · p780
questions.q: A patient with RPGN has an ABG showing metabolic acidosis. Which treatments are listed in the algorithm?
opts: Oral alkali with potassium binders only
questions.exp: ABG showing metabolic acidosis is treated with NaHCO₃ or dialysis. (Book p780)

questions.sec: RPGN treatment approach: check first · p780
questions.q: Match the volume-status assessment with its treatment — 1) Assessment  2) Treatment … A) Diuretics  B) Check inferior vena cava diameter on USG
questions.exp: Volume status is assessed by the inferior vena cava diameter on USG, and diuretics are the treatment used for the volume problem. (Book p780)

questions.sec: RPGN treatment approach: check first · p780
questions.q: The first step in managing RPGN, before specific therapy, is to check the ECG, ABG and volume status.
opts: False — ECG is checked only after dialysis
False — ABG is checked only after biopsy
True, but only in type I RPGN
questions.exp: Treatment approach, step 1: check ECG for hyperkalaemia, ABG for metabolic acidosis and volume status by IVC diameter on USG. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: All of the following are absolute (uremic) indications for dialysis EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Absolute uremic indications: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding and gastritis. Volume overload is a relative indication, along with hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis resistant to treatment. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Fill up: The absolute indications for dialysis in RPGN are all ______ in nature.
questions.exp: Absolute indications for dialysis = uremic: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding, gastritis. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Match the indication type with its items — 1) Absolute indication  2) Relative indication … A) Volume overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis — when resistant to treatment  B) Uremic encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding
questions.exp: Absolute (uremic) indications: encephalopathy, halitosis, pruritis, pericarditis, bleeding, gastritis. Relative indications: volume overload, hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis that are resistant to treatment. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Hyperkalaemia in RPGN is an absolute indication for dialysis regardless of whether it responds to medical treatment.
opts: False — hyperkalaemia is a relative indication and must be resistant to treatment
True — hyperkalaemia is always an absolute uremic indication
True, but only if the ECG is normal
False — dialysis is never indicated for hyperkalaemia
questions.exp: Hyperkalaemia appears along with volume overload and metabolic acidosis under relative indications, qualified as resistant to treatment. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: On the basis of immunofluorescence, RPGN is classified into:
opts: Three types — I, II and III
Two types — granular and linear only
Four types — I, II, III and IV
Five types including double-positive and double-negative
questions.exp: The TYPES flowchart of RPGN begins 'on the basis of immunofluorescence' and branches into type I (Goodpasture syndrome), type II (immune complex) and type III (pauci-immune). Types IV/V appear only inside the later double-positive vs double-negative table. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Type I RPGN is also known as:
questions.exp: Type I / Goodpasture syndrome: IF shows linear IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Fill up: Type I RPGN shows ______ IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall on immunofluorescence.
questions.exp: Type I RPGN (Goodpasture syndrome) IF: linear IgG ± C3 in the capillary wall. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Match the RPGN type with its mechanism — 1) Type II  2) Type III … A) Pauci-immune  B) Immune complex deposition
questions.exp: Type II RPGN = immune complex deposition (commonest below 20 years of age); type III RPGN = pauci-immune (the commonest overall type). (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Type II RPGN is commonest in patients:
questions.exp: Type II RPGN is annotated 'm/c in <20 yrs age' within the immune-complex branch. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: A 16-year-old girl has RPGN with immune-complex deposition on biopsy. Which example fits the book's type II list best?
questions.exp: Type II (immune complex) examples: SLE — underlined as the most important cause — Henoch–Schönlein purpura, IPGN (IgA predominant) and membranoproliferative GN (10%). (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Systemic lupus erythematosus is marked as the most important cause within the type II RPGN examples.
opts: False — HSP is the most important cause
False — MPGN is the most important cause
True, but only above 60 years of age
questions.exp: In the type II branch, SLE is underlined with the note '(most important cause)'; HSP, IPGN (IgA predominant) and MPGN (10%) complete the list. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Which example does NOT belong to the type II (immune complex) group of RPGN?
questions.exp: Microscopic polyangiitis belongs to type III (pauci-immune) with ANCA vasculitis and Wegener's granulomatosis. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Match the type II examples with the bracketed note given beside them — 1) Henoch–Schönlein purpura and IPGN  2) Membranoproliferative GN … A) Listed as (10%)  B) Marked as the 'adult variety'
questions.exp: In the type II list, HSP and IPGN (IgA predominant) are bracketed together as the adult variety, while MPGN carries the figure 10%. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Type III RPGN is described as:
opts: Immune complex disease — commonest below 20 years
A disease seen only in children
questions.exp: Type III (pauci-immune) is marked m/c, i.e. the commonest type of RPGN, with examples ANCA vasculitis, Wegener's granulomatosis and microscopic polyangiitis. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Which of these is NOT among the examples of type III (pauci-immune) RPGN?
questions.exp: IPGN (IgA predominant) is listed under type II immune-complex RPGN; type III pauci-immune examples are ANCA vasculitis, Wegener's granulomatosis and microscopic polyangiitis. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Match each RPGN type with its expected ANCA/anti-GBM serology from the double-positive vs double-negative table — 1) Type IV (double positive)  2) Type V (double negative) … A) Anti-GBM – and ANCA –  B) Anti-GBM + and ANCA +
questions.exp: The table: type IV = double positive (anti-GBM antibody +, ANCA +); type V = double negative (anti-GBM antibody –, ANCA –). (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: Prognosis is good in double-positive (type IV) RPGN and poor in double-negative (type V) RPGN.
opts: False — prognosis is poor in type IV and good in type V
False — prognosis is identical in both
True, but only when C3 is low
questions.exp: The table's prognosis row reads good for type IV (double positive) and poor for type V (double negative). (Book p780)

questions.sec: Dialysis indications & RPGN types · p780
questions.q: A patient with RPGN has both anti-GBM antibody and ANCA positive on serology. According to the table he has:
opts: Type IV RPGN — with a good prognosis
Type V RPGN — with a poor prognosis
Type I RPGN — with a poor prognosis
Type III RPGN — with a poor prognosis
questions.exp: Type IV = double positive (anti-GBM + and ANCA +), and this carries a good prognosis; type V (double negative) has a poor prognosis. (Book p780)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: Pulmonary renal syndrome is defined as:
opts: RPGN (kidney involvement) plus diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (lung involvement)
Nephrotic syndrome plus pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction
Acute kidney injury plus cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with pleural effusion
Chronic kidney disease plus obstructive sleep apnoea with nocturnal hypoxaemia
questions.exp: Pulmonary renal syndrome = RPGN (kidney involvement) + diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (lung involvement). (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: All of the following are listed conditions under pulmonary renal syndrome EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Conditions listed: Goodpasture syndrome, microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and SLE (active disease). PSGN is not listed here. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: Active SLE is listed as one of the conditions causing pulmonary renal syndrome.
opts: False — SLE causes only nephrotic syndrome
True, but only in drug-induced lupus
False — SLE is excluded because C3 is normal
questions.exp: The conditions list for pulmonary renal syndrome ends with SLE (active disease). (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: According to the note, RPGN with diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and a non-specific antibody is:
opts: SLE with class V lupus nephritis
questions.exp: Note: RPGN + DAH + antibody (non-specific) = anti-GBM disease; the antibody in question is anti-GBM. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: Fill up: Goodpasture disease is RPGN + diffuse alveolar haemorrhage + antibody against the noncollagenous domain of the ______ chain of type-IV collagen.
questions.exp: Goodpasture disease = RPGN + DAH + antibody against the noncollagenous domain of the α3 chain of type-IV collagen. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: Match the pulmonary trigger with its appearance in the Goodpasture disease notes — 1) Smoking  2) Hydrocarbon exposure  3) Fluid overload  4) Lung infection … A) All four are listed 2nd/trigger factors
opts: Only smoking and lung infection are triggers
Only fluid overload is a trigger
questions.exp: 2nd/trigger factors for Goodpasture disease: smoking, hydrocarbon exposure, fluid overload and lung infection. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: Which is NOT a listed trigger for Goodpasture disease?
questions.exp: Listed triggers: smoking, hydrocarbon exposure, fluid overload and lung infection. A streptococcal sore throat relates to PSGN, not Goodpasture disease. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: Match the HLA group with its risk in Goodpasture disease — 1) High risk  2) Low risk … A) DR1, DR7  B) DR2/15, DR4
questions.exp: HLA association in Goodpasture disease: high risk DR2/15 and DR4; low risk DR1 and DR7. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: A 25-year-old heavy smoker has haemoptysis, a fall in Hb and rapidly rising creatinine; anti-GBM antibody is positive. Which HLA type would be expected to increase his risk?
questions.exp: High-risk HLA types in Goodpasture disease are DR2/15 and DR4; DR1 and DR7 are low risk. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Pulmonary renal syndrome & Goodpasture HLA · p781
questions.q: Which HLA type is protective/low-risk in Goodpasture disease rather than high-risk?
questions.exp: Low-risk HLA types: DR1 and DR7. High risk: DR2/15 and DR4. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome · p781
questions.q: The first session of dialysis should be kept shorter than:
questions.exp: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome: the first session of dialysis should be <1 hour, with subsequent sessions of 4 hours. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome · p781
questions.q: The duration of subsequent dialysis sessions recommended after the first short session is:
questions.exp: First session <1 hour; subsequent sessions 4 hours, to avoid dialysis disequilibrium syndrome. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome · p781
questions.q: Complete the dialysis disequilibrium flowchart — 1) Urea in the blood compartment  2) Effect on blood osmolality  3) Consequence in cells … A) Cerebral edema → seizure, death  B) Rapidly moves to the dialysate compartment  C) ↓ Osmolality
questions.exp: Flowchart: urea rapidly moves from blood to dialysate → blood osmolality falls → water moves into cells → cerebral oedema → seizure and death. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome · p781
questions.q: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome occurs because urea is removed so quickly that the osmolality of the blood compartment falls.
opts: False — blood osmolality rises during dialysis
False — the syndrome is caused by water leaving the cells
True, but the fall in osmolality causes intracellular dehydration
questions.exp: Urea moves rapidly into the dialysate, dropping blood osmolality; water then moves into cells, producing cerebral oedema with seizure and death if dialysis is continued beyond 2 hours. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome · p781
questions.q: A severely uraemic patient receives a 4-hour first dialysis session and develops headache, confusion and a seizure. The mechanism is:
opts: Water movement into cells after a rapid fall in blood osmolality — cerebral edema
Rapid movement of water out of cells causing cerebral dehydration
questions.exp: Dialysis disequilibrium: rapid urea removal → ↓ blood osmolality → water moves into cells (including brain) → cerebral oedema, seizure and death. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome · p781
questions.q: Which statement correctly summarises the prevention of dialysis disequilibrium syndrome?
opts: Limit the first dialysis session to less than 1 hour, with 4-hour subsequent sessions
Give the first session for 6 hours to clear urea completely
Avoid dialysis in uraemic patients altogether
Use only peritoneal dialysis in all uraemic patients
questions.exp: Prevention: the first dialysis session should be <1 hour; subsequent sessions are 4 hours, because continuing beyond 2 hours risks cerebral oedema. (Book p781)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: Lung involvement (as opposed to renal involvement) occurs in what proportion of Goodpasture patients?
questions.exp: Presentation flowchart: lung involvement 75% versus renal involvement 'as %', with renal involvement indicating a poor prognosis. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: In Goodpasture syndrome, renal involvement is associated with a poor prognosis.
opts: False — only lung involvement affects prognosis
True only if the patient smokes
questions.exp: The flowchart places 'renal involvement (as %)' with the note poor prognosis. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: A young man presents with 2 weeks of cough and haemoptysis. He has no fever and no comorbidity. Which listed feature supports the diagnosis of Goodpasture lung involvement?
opts: Haemoptysis with no fever or comorbidity, in a smoker
Pleuritic chest pain with a pleural rub
questions.exp: Lung features: history of smoking, cough, haemoptysis, and no fever or comorbidity — the absence of fever is emphasised. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed lung features of Goodpasture syndrome. Which is the odd one out?
questions.exp: The book specifically notes 'no fever, comorbidity' among the lung features of Goodpasture syndrome. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: Match the investigation with its stated result — 1) DLCO  2) X-ray chest  3) CT scan … A) B/L diffuse infiltrate  B) ↑ (increased)  C) Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
questions.exp: Evaluation: DLCO is ↑ (increased); X-ray shows bilateral diffuse infiltrate; CT scan shows diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: The chest X-ray in Goodpasture syndrome shows a bilateral diffuse infiltrate, marked by an arrow in the figure.
opts: False — the X-ray is normal in Goodpasture syndrome
False — the X-ray shows a solitary cavitating lesion
True, but only after renal transplantation
questions.exp: The chest X-ray figure is labelled 'B/L diffuse infiltrate' with an arrow pointing to it. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: A patient with haemoptysis and RPGN has a CT chest showing bilateral ground-glass with dependent consolidation. The figure labels this:
questions.exp: The two CT panels on the page are labelled 'diffuse alveolar haemorrhage'. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture presentation & evaluation · p782
questions.q: Which evaluation finding is NOT part of the Goodpasture work-up as printed?
questions.exp: The DLCO in Goodpasture syndrome is increased (↑), reflecting the presence of blood in the alveoli; X-ray shows B/L diffuse infiltrate and CT shows diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture active management, treatment & transplant note · p782
questions.q: All of the following are conditions requiring active management in pulmonary renal syndrome EXCEPT:
opts: Positive ANCA serology with fibrous crescents only
Sr. creatinine <5.5 mg/dL with normal urine output
questions.exp: Conditions requiring active management: ongoing pulmonary haemorrhage; Sr. creatinine <5.5 mg/dL with normal urine output; new cellular (non-fibrous) crescent; and type IV RPGN. (Book p782)

questions.sec: Goodpasture active management, treatment & transplant note · p782
questions.q: The serum creatinine cut-off below which active management is indicated, provided urine output is normal, is:
questions.exp: Condition 2 requiring active management: Sr. creatinine <5.5 mg/dL with normal urine output. (Book p782)

units.title: Renal failure flowchart, RPRF causes & RPGN features
units.guide: Renal failure divides into CKD and non-CKD; non-CKD splits by speed into AKI (hours–days) and RPRF (days–weeks). RPRF is caused by RPGN (glomerular pathology), HUS, severe acute interstitial nephritis and (some cases of) atheroembolic renal disease. RPGN itself = RPRF + diffuse proliferative GN with crescents. Learn the urine protein, oedema compartment and the laboratory panel.

units.title: RPGN biopsy: crescents, IF patterns and the dialysis-first rule
units.guide: Light microscopy: parietal epithelial proliferation with fibrin crescents (number matters). Immunofluorescence: negative, diffuse granular, linear and granular panels — linear IF marking type I RPGN, with associations Goodpasture disease (linear), diabetes mellitus and light chain disease (granular). Never biopsy a markedly raised creatinine at once: dialyse, recheck and only then biopsy.

units.title: RPGN treatment approach, dialysis indications & types I–V
units.guide: Step 1 checks: ECG (hyperkalaemia → calcium gluconate 10 mL IV over 2–3 min), ABG (metabolic acidosis → NaHCO₃ or dialysis) and volume status (IVC diameter → diuretics). Absolute dialysis indications are uremic; relative ones are resistant volume overload, hyperkalaemia and acidosis. IF-based types: I Goodpasture (linear), II immune complex (<20 years, SLE most important), III pauci-immune (commonest), plus the double-positive type IV (good prognosis) versus double-negative type V (poor prognosis) table.

units.title: Pulmonary renal syndrome, Goodpasture HLA and dialysis disequilibrium
units.guide: Pulmonary renal syndrome = RPGN + diffuse alveolar haemorrhage; list Goodpasture, microscopic polyangiitis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and active SLE. Goodpasture disease targets the noncollagenous domain of the α3 chain of type-IV collagen with triggers smoking, hydrocarbons, fluid overload and lung infection; DR2/15 and DR4 are high risk, DR1 and DR7 low risk. Dialysis disequilibrium: first session <1 hour, subsequent 4 hours, else ↓osmolality drives water into cells → cerebral oedema, seizure, death.

units.title: Goodpasture presentation, work-up, treatment and post-transplant notes
units.guide: Lung involvement in 75% with cough, haemoptysis, smoking history and no fever; renal involvement means poor prognosis. DLCO is increased, X-ray shows B/L diffuse infiltrate and CT shows diffuse alveolar haemorrhage. Active management for ongoing pulmonary haemorrhage, creatinine <5.5 mg/dL with normal urine output, new cellular crescent and type IV RPGN; mainstay PLEX + steroid/cyclophosphamide for 3–6 months; transplant after 6 months of antibody negativity. Goodpasture does not recur post-transplant, whereas Alport syndrome carries a 5% risk of post-transplant Goodpasture syndrome.
